name: Khengkha
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ikeda, Takumi. 2021. An Introduction to Khengkha: A Language of Central Bhutan. In Nagano Yasuhiko & Ikeda Takumi (eds.), Grammatical Phenomena of Sino-Tibetan Languages 4: Link Languages and Archetypes in Tibeto-Burman, 71-119. Kyoto: Institute for Research in Humanities, Kyoto University. hdl:2433/263978 (open access, KURENAI).
catalog_quote: The common phonological features observed over the sub-dialects of Khengkha consist of a five main vowel system, pitch accent systems, a restricted set of final consonants, and a restricted set of consonant clusters in initials. It is still premature to describe the phonological system and features in detail; this report can only provide first-hand data and a preliminary analysis. The Khengkha phonological system has not been established yet, therefore, I tried to use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) to record and describe the phonetic appearance in detail. I think it will be better than using the provisional phonemic system in the Roman Alphabet, which would be an unstable scheme inductively made of restricted data.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Phonology', word for word as reported: 'The common phonological features observed over the sub-dialects of Khengkha consist of a five main vowel system, pitch accent systems, a restricted set of final consonants, and a restricted set of consonant clusters in initials. It is still premature to describe the phonological system and features in detail; this report can only provide first-hand data and a preliminary analysis. The Khengkha phonological system has not been established yet, therefore, I tried to use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) to record and describe the phonetic appearance…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement says Khengkha has a 'pitch accent system' (shared by all its sub-dialects) but explicitly declines to analyse it; no rule for which syllable carries the accent is given. Pitch is transcribed syllable by syllable with Chao numerals throughout the sketch and the 121-page wordlist (e.g. ŋɑ²¹ 'I', ʔo⁴⁴lo²² 'child', jɑː²³ŋʌ²² 'five'); the nearest related descriptions (Michailovsky & Mazaudon 1994 for Kurtoep/Bumthap; Dorji 2022 fn. 3 for Khengkha) point to a high/low register distinction tied to initial consonants, not to a stress-placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author states the phonology has not yet been established and the analysis is preliminary.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms in a wordlist and elicited sentences); dialects sampled: Trongsa, Trong and Wamling (Zhemgang). The statement is a type statement (pitch accent present) rather than a placement rule; it should be catalogued as 'pitch accent, placement undescribed'.
new_statements.identity_note: Ikeda 2021 describes Khengkha proper (khen1241) from three sub-dialects (Trongsa; Trong and Wamling in Zhemgang), so identity matches. Michailovsky & Mazaudon 1994 (held by the project) describes Kurtoep (kurt1248) and Bumthap (bumt1240), not Kheng, and must not be attributed to khen1241. Dorji 2022 is Khengkha (Taktse, Trongsa speaker).

When tone does not fit this pattern, it is marked as such. For example, high tone will be marked following voiced sonorants and low tone will be marked following voiceless obstruetns.

sources.note: Sec. 2 Phonology (p. 73) lists 'pitch accent systems' among the common phonological features of all Khengkha sub-dialects, then says it is 'still premature to describe the phonological system and features in detail'; no rule for where the accent/stress falls is given anywhere. Every syllable in the data is transcribed with Chao pitch numerals (e.g. ŋɑ²¹ 'I', mi²¹ 'person', ʔo⁴⁴lo²² 'child'); 2.1-2.3 cover consonants, vowels, diphthongs/codas only. The 49-page text was searched for stress/accent/tone/pitch/prosody: the p. 73 sentence is the only hit.

sources.note: Phonology section is on Kurtoep (kurt1248) with notes on Bumthap proper: 'two tonal registers, high and low, correlated with voicing oppositions in the initial consonant' (p. 546); 'Tone register (high vs low): A high vs low contrast is found on words with nasal or continuant initials..' (p. 547). No Kheng data: Khengke is mentioned only as 'by all reports' mutually intelligible with Kurtoep and Bumthap (p. 545). Nothing on stress. Context for the group only, not a Khengkha description.

sources.note: Comparative lexical/morphological paper; fn. 1 states the transcription convention for all East Bodish data incl. Khengkha: tone predictable (high after voiceless, low after voiced onsets) and marked only where unpredictable, i.e. high after sonorants / low after voiceless obstruents; Khengkha forms accordingly carry marked high tone after sonorant onsets, e.g. Kh ɲéŋ 'year', nyít 'seven' (p. 5-6) vs unmarked kwa 'tooth', mek 'eye'. No Khengkha-specific tone discussion beyond the data.

No inventory table, no rule, a passing remark only.
